title: Quicksort 2 - Sorting (Partition)
directAnswer: Take the partition step from Quicksort 1 and apply it recursively: pivot = first element, split into left (< pivot) and right (≥ pivot), recursively sort each, then combine as `sort(left) + [pivot] + sort(right)`. Print the combined sub-array after each combine whose length is greater than 1. Base case: a sub-array of length ≤ 1 is already sorted (and is not printed).

remember.pattern: Recursive quicksort built on the single-partition step
remember.formula:
def qsort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    p = a[0]
    left  = [x for x in a[1:] if x < p]
    right = [x for x in a[1:] if x >= p]
    res = qsort(left) + [p] + qsort(right)
    print(res)        # only fires for len(res) > 1
    return res
rules: Recurse on **both** sides — that is the only difference from Quicksort 1, which partitions once.
Print the combined array **after** the recursive calls return, so what you print is partially (sub-)sorted, not raw.
Only print when the combined sub-array has length > 1; length-1 sub-arrays are base cases and are never printed.
Pivot is the first element of each sub-array; route equals consistently (here `≥ pivot` goes right) so no element is lost.
The LAST printed line is always the fully sorted array (the top-level combine).
whenToUse: You must fully sort and also show intermediate progress of a divide-and-conquer sort
Demonstrating how partition composes into a sort
A teaching / tracing context where each merge of sorted halves is observable
antiSignals: You only need one partition, not a sort → Quicksort 1
You need guaranteed O(n log n) worst case → heapsort or mergesort, not quicksort
You only need the k-th element → quickselect (recurse one side)
remember.takeaway: Quicksort = partition + recurse on both halves. Printing each combine reveals the divide-and-conquer tree: small sorted pieces appear first, the full array last.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can compose the single partition step into a correct recursion with a proper base case, and reason about the order in which sub-arrays become sorted.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recursing on only one side, missing the length ≤ 1 base case (infinite recursion or printing singletons), or printing the raw partition before the recursive calls return.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain that printing after the combine shows partially sorted state, identify that the deepest-left combine prints first, and note the O(n²) worst case when the pivot is always the min/max.

problemStatement:
Using the partition logic from Quicksort 1, implement a recursive quicksort that fully sorts the array.

The pivot for each sub-array is its first element. After sorting a sub-array (combining its sorted left part, the pivot, and its sorted right part), print that sub-array — but only when it has more than one element.

The final line printed is the fully sorted array.
constraints: Elements are distinct in the challenge inputs
Pivot is always the first element of the current sub-array
understanding: Quicksort 1 placed one pivot. Quicksort 2 repeats that recursively: after partitioning, both the left and right sides are themselves sorted by the same routine, then stitched back together. Printing the stitched result after each recursive return lets you watch the array assemble itself bottom-up, smallest pieces first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I recurse on both sides?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Quicksort 1 partitions once; Quicksort 2 recursively sorts both the left and right partitions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: When exactly do I print?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: After combining sort(left) + [pivot] + sort(right), and only when that combined array has more than one element.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What is the base case?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A sub-array of length 0 or 1 is already sorted — return it as-is and do not print.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Where does an element equal to the pivot go?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Pick a consistent side (here ≥ pivot goes right). The challenge inputs are distinct, but a consistent rule prevents losing duplicates in general.

examples.explanation: Pivot 5 → left [1,3,2], right [8,7,9]. Sorting the left sub-array prints '2 3' then '1 2 3'; sorting the right prints '7 8 9'; the top-level combine prints the full sorted array.
Pivot 4 → left [3,2] sorts to '2 3'; right [5,7] sorts to '5 7'; top combine prints '2 3 4 5 7'.

approaches.name: Recursive Quicksort with Helper Arrays (Intended)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution — it reuses Quicksort 1's partition and makes the print points obvious.

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

hints: You already have a one-step partition. What if each side were itself partitioned the same way?
Write a function that partitions around arr[0] into left (<p) and right (≥p), then returns sort(left) + [p] + sort(right).
Add the base case len ≤ 1 (return as-is). Print the combined result right before returning, only when its length > 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each level of recursion does O(n) partition work across all sub-arrays; with balanced pivots there are O(log n) levels → O(n log n). A sorted input with first-element pivots gives one-sided splits, O(n) levels → O(n²). Helper arrays plus recursion stack cost O(n log n) space on average.
approaches.explanation:
This is Quicksort 1's partition wrapped in recursion. For a sub-array, set `p = a[0]`, route the remaining elements into `left` (`< p`) and `right` (`≥ p`), then return `qsort(left) + [p] + qsort(right)`.

**Why recursing both sides sorts the array.** After partitioning, `p` is in its final sorted position (everything left is smaller, everything right is larger). Recursively sorting each side places every element correctly, so the concatenation is fully sorted. This is the divide-and-conquer guarantee.

**Why the print shows partially sorted state.** The print runs *after* `qsort(left)` and `qsort(right)` have returned, so `left` and `right` are already sorted when we stitch and print. The very first line printed is the deepest-left combine (the smallest sub-array to finish), and the very last is the top-level combine — the entire sorted array. Tracing `[5,8,1,3,7,9,2]` you get `2 3`, then `1 2 3`, then `7 8 9`, then `1 2 3 5 7 8 9`.

**Why the `len ≤ 1` base case and the `> 1` print guard.** A sub-array of size 0 or 1 is already sorted, so we return immediately — this also stops the recursion. We skip printing singletons because the challenge only wants combines of genuine sub-arrays (length > 1), matching how partitions of size 1 don't represent real merge work.

**Why route equals to one side.** Using `≥ p` for the right side guarantees every non-pivot element lands in exactly one bucket even when duplicates exist; dropping the equals case would silently lose elements.
approaches.insight: Quicksort is 'partition, then trust recursion for both halves'. The print order is a free visualisation of the call stack unwinding — leaves resolve first, the root last. Recognising that post-order print = bottom-up assembly is the same insight behind printing a merge sort's merges.

dryRun.intro: Pivot is the first element of each sub-array. Prints happen after each combine of length > 1, deepest-left first.

Same partition as Quicksort 1; equals go right via the else branch so no element is lost.
Recurse on the left FIRST, so its prints appear before the right and before this level's combine.
Print the combined, partially-sorted sub-array — only when length > 1.

python.line: right = [x for x in a[1:] if x >= p]
python.explanation: Route equals to the right consistently so duplicates aren't dropped.
Combine happens after both recursive calls return, so res is sorted when printed.
Post-order print reveals smaller sorted pieces before the full array.

pitfalls: Recursing on only one side — leaves the other side unsorted.
Missing the len ≤ 1 base case — infinite recursion or stack overflow.
Printing the raw partition before the recursive calls return — prints unsorted instead of sorted sub-arrays.
Printing length-1 sub-arrays — violates the 'only length > 1' rule.

edgeCases.behavior: Already sorted; first-element pivots give one-sided splits — prints '2 3' then '1 2 3' (O(n²) shape).

approaches.name: In-Place Lomuto Quicksort (Space-Optimised)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring up when asked how production quicksort sorts without allocating arrays at every level.

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

hints: Can you sort without building new left/right lists at each level?
Partition the sub-array [lo..hi] in place around a pivot, returning the pivot's final index pIdx.
Recurse on [lo..pIdx-1] and [pIdx+1..hi]. Print the sub-array slice after both recursive calls if hi - lo + 1 > 1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: In-place partition is O(length) per call; balanced recursion gives O(n log n) total, degenerate pivots give O(n²). Only the recursion stack uses extra space: O(log n) average, O(n) worst.
approaches.explanation:
Instead of allocating helper lists, partition the current slice in place. Lomuto's scheme keeps a boundary `i`; scanning `j` over the slice, smaller-than-pivot elements are swapped toward the front, then the pivot is swapped into the boundary, which becomes its final index `pIdx`. Recurse on the two sub-slices.

**Why it saves memory.** No new arrays per level — all work happens within the original array, so only the recursion stack costs space (`O(log n)` when balanced). This is what real library quicksorts do.

**Why printing is trickier here.** The 'partially sorted concatenation' the challenge wants corresponds to the out-of-place combine. To reproduce the exact same printed lines, you'd print the slice `[lo..hi]` after both recursive calls return and only when its length > 1 — but the in-place pivot placement (and equal-element handling) can yield a different internal arrangement than the helper-array version. If the grader expects the specific helper-array order, prefer the first approach; use this one when only the final sorted array (or in-place behaviour) is being graded.
approaches.insight: The choice between out-of-place and in-place quicksort is the classic time/space-vs-clarity trade. Helper arrays make the partition and print points obvious; in-place Lomuto is leaner but its intermediate states differ. Pick the version that matches what's being graded.

Pivot lands at its final sorted index in place.

python.explanation: First element of the slice is the pivot, matching the challenge.

pitfalls: Using lo >= hi vs lo > hi inconsistently — both work, but mixing them causes off-by-one bugs.
Forgetting to exclude the pivot index when recursing (sort(lo, pIdx) loops forever).
Expecting identical printed intermediate lines to the helper-array version — the in-place arrangement can differ.

edgeCases.behavior: Sorted input → pivot always the min → fully one-sided recursion, O(n²) but correct: [1,2,3].
Reverse sorted → still sorts correctly to [1,2,3] in O(n²).

commonMistakes: Recursing on only one partition side, leaving part of the array unsorted.
Omitting the length ≤ 1 base case, causing infinite recursion.
Printing the partition before the recursive calls return — shows unsorted sub-arrays.
Printing single-element sub-arrays despite the 'length > 1' rule.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Printing before recursion (wrong order)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The challenge wants the partially SORTED sub-array. Printing right after partition shows the raw, unsorted split instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
p = a[0]
left = [x for x in a[1:] if x < p]
right = [x for x in a[1:] if x >= p]
print(' '.join(map(str, left + [p] + right)))  # raw split
res = qsort(left) + [p] + qsort(right)
return res
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
p = a[0]
left = [x for x in a[1:] if x < p]
right = [x for x in a[1:] if x >= p]
res = qsort(left) + [p] + qsort(right)
if len(res) > 1:
    print(' '.join(map(str, res)))  # sorted sub-array
return res

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the base case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without returning on len ≤ 1, the recursion never bottoms out and singletons also get printed, violating the spec.
